- A minimal example that uses vertex color (thus supporting `SpriteBase3D.modulate`) and the albedo texture is attached.

Note that `ShaderCreateDialog` doesn't seem to support adding custom shader templates in the first place, so I've taken the liberty to make it a bit easier to add hardcoded shader templates. Perhaps a future feature proposal could expand on this and make it more similar to script templates in terms of ergonomics.

Just looking at this because it came up during the rendering meeting, with clay on holiday don't want to make an in-depth judgement call.

But my question would be, why make this work with a special uniform? Why not make this work with the normal albedo color hint so the code is the same as with normal geometry? What makes this a different situation?

> Just looking at this because it came up during the rendering meeting, with clay on holiday don't want to make an in-depth judgement call.
> 
> But my question would be, why make this work with a special uniform? Why not make this work with the normal albedo color hint so the code is the same as with normal geometry? What makes this a different situation?

Oh, I was admittedly not aware of the `source_color` hint's existence.

The design here was so the code path is consistent between both cases. `texture_albedo` and `texture_albedo_size` are both uniforms that are configured for the default Sprite3D material. (`StandardMaterial3D::get_material_for_2d`)

I see how it's possible to replace `texture_albedo` by looking for a sampler2D uniform with `HINT_SOURCE_COLOR` instead. There isn't an equivalent hint for `texture_albedo_size`, however.

Though `texture_albedo_size` is only used to [calculate the MSDF](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/594d64ec244b6b99321e2096987d4d69de4c8845/scene/resources/material.cpp#L1511) and is technically optional. (My example there didn't use it either) So we could just not set `texture_albedo_size` for custom materials. What do you think?

@BastiaanOlij

(Rebased to fix conflict with https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/ad9b66100e64d31019624c8eefeb5dbee738f3b5 )

Follow up: I think there's an actual argument *against* using `HINT_SOURCE_COLOR` (corresponding to the `source_color` hint) here.
- A quick search into the engine's source code shows that there's no existing code that looks for a uniform with a specific hint and assigns values to it.
- `HINT_SOURCE_COLOR` is mostly used so Godot knows to make a texture work as a color texture.
  - It's not even possible to retrieve this information at the moment. [`ShaderLanguage::uniform_to_property_info`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/e531f3eb7b13a9adaaf5b15ac9b3aebc4c2030cd/servers/rendering/shader_language.cpp#L4808) (used by `RenderingServer::get_shader_parameter_list`) is unable to include this information and we can't tell if a sampler2D uniform is `source_color`, `hint_normal`, or some other hint.
  - Even if we could, this would mean that uniform order now matters and if someone has multiple `source_color` uniforms, they must be aware that the first will be assigned the sprite texture by Sprite3D.

As such, I think the current approach is fine as-is.

It's been a long time, but I've revised my approach and made my implementation much more clean. I'm also fresh out of a game jam where I had to hack my own Sprite3D shader in by passing the texture to the material override every frame so I'd love to push this PR forward again. That aside... https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/71fa960f-679b-4e75-ad32-c18f2cd116c0 (Sorry for the compression rate) # What's changed Instead of relying on `GeometryInstance3D.material_override`, the property `SpriteBase3D.custom_material` has been added instead. This avoids having to make changes to `GeometryInstance3D` to add a signal that detects when the material override is changed, and gives us better control overall. Validation is of course added for `custom_material`. Notably, custom materials are automatically made unique in the editor when assigned. The `Sprite3D` shader template has also been adjusted. I had to copy the SRGB conversion code verbatim but now using the template gives you pretty much identical results to a stock `SpriteBase3D` and should be a good starting point for most users. One major limitation remaining is that there's no easy way to override the custom AABB set by `SpriteBase3D`. My implementation disables the billboard AABB code when `custom_material` is assigned, so if the user reimplements billboards in their shader they'd have to find a way to defer their `set_custom_aabb()` call until after `SpriteBase3D` is redrawn, or just set it every frame and hope it sticks. But this is a limitation with `SpriteBase3D` even before this PR, so I'll hold off from addressing this issue for now.

Design Details

Why not a custom_shader instead of custom_material?

A `custom_shader` would fit `SpriteBase3D`'s internal design better, allowing us to use the same material instance created by every `SpriteBase3D`. But there are editor limitations that make this approach not very practical. Most importantly, a plain `Shader` property does not get to use the same `EditorShaderPicker` used by `ShaderMaterial` in the inspector. This means you can't actually select shader templates on the spot if `custom_shader` is used instead of `custom_material`, and I believe this would be bad UX. It _is_ a strange limitation but implementing an `EditorResourcePicker` that shows `ShaderCreateDialog` for every shader property is way too much work and out of the scope of this PR. I've gone as far as implementing my own inspector plugin for `SpriteBase3D` before realizing that I'd also have to reimplement how `ShaderMaterial` exposes shader parameters (allowing `AnimationMixer` to modify them) and that's where I gave up.

What's wrong with using material overrides?

`SpriteBase3D` doesn't actually respect the "mesh instance" system provided by `GeometryInstance3D` to begin with. It has its own material instance for example. But more importantly, `SpriteBase3D` *expects* that it gets to use a unique material. Letting `SpriteBase3D` own the custom material directly instead of via `GeometryInstance3D` makes UX improvements like guaranteeing material uniqueness much easier. It also lets me inform the user directly via the custom material's documentation that the material has to be unique. This would be much less obvious with material overrides since it's otherwise perfectly normal to reuse material overrides across `MeshInstance3D` for example.

You're assigning texture_albedo and albedo_texture_size to custom_material. Wouldn't this be redundant data?

Yes. This is unfortunately a limitation with how property info works. I'd love to disable those two shader parameters in particular by changing their property usages, but as it stands this is impossible without hacking into `ShaderMaterial`. It's as hacky as it sounds so I'd like to avoid doing so for now. This category of issues affects many other Godot features such as AnimationMixer's animation playback in-editor anyway.

After reviewing the custom AABB code and examining other `mesh_set_custom_aabb()` usages, I realized that this is completely unnecessary to begin with, since `SpriteBase3D` already overrides `VisualInstance3D::get_mesh()` and returns a copy of the custom AABB.

This means `SpriteBase3D` is no longer secretly overwriting the custom AABB, and this removes the last major limitation of this PR.
